#4215. 9 PS5 RPGs Where You’re Actually the Villain

Eric Warner is a Journalist and Multimedia Producer based in New England with over 7 years of experience producing stories for multiple publications

Most video game narratives typically have players embody heroic roles, such as Link in The Legend of Zelda series, but several games do allow people to adopt more villainous roles.

This is especially seen in role-playing games, as they offer players the chance to go down heroic paths, neutral paths, or even downright diabolical ones, with some of the best RPGs featuring karma systems that track good and back actions and have characters and factions respond to players’ choices.

While some RPGs still push players towards acting heroically, here are nine RPGs available on the PlayStation 5 that allow people to play completely villainous roles and wreak havoc. Naturally, there are big spoilers ahead for these titles, so beware if you haven't played them yet!

Warhorse Studios’ Kingdom Come: Deliverance surprised many players in 2018 by depicting an engaging, realistic medieval RPG centered around the Bohemian commoner turned hero Henry, as he sets out to avenge his family and join Lord Radzig Kobyla in fighting invading forces.

Henry’s story continues in the recently released Kingdom Come: Deliverance II, but Warhorse Studios granted players more freedom in how to control Henry’s life and how he interacts with NPCs. Players are able to keep Henry on the path of a hero or have him become a complete jerk.

For instance, Henry can tattle on people to authorities resulting in their imprisonment or death, sabotage businesses, and commit various crimes, with these diabolical actions ending up with the spirits of Henry’s parents disavowing him from the afterlife.

Some of the best RPGs to play as a villain in are those created by Bethesda, and luckily Virtuos remastered one Bethesda’s best RPGs for modern platforms with The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion Remastered.

Like many Elder Scrolls games, The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion Remastered starts with players embodying an unnamed prisoner destined for greatness, but they can quickly ignore that grand destiny and go about slaying almost everyone in Cyrodiil.

Players can even go so far as to join the Dark Brotherhood, a merciless cult of shadowy assassins, and take part in several contracted killings, such as staging a fatal accident to kill the innocent Wood Elf Baenlin and wiping out every living member in a family.

PlayStation 4 players who want play adventure titles that feature villains as protagonists should check out these 10 games.

Obsidian Entertainment is widely regarded to be one of the best RPG developers in modern gaming, having created Fallout: New Vegas, South Park: The Stick of Truth, and The Outer Worlds, with one of their better RPGs available on PS5 so far being Avowed.

A first and third-person fantasy RPG, Avowed has players embody a character simply known as the Envoy as they journey to the Living Lands region of Eora, to investigate a mysterious plague known as the Dream Scourge and confront several factions vying for control over the region.

Easily the most evil faction in the region is the Steel Garrote, a corrupt order of paladins, and, if players chose to kill the assassin Ygwulf, allow the Garrote to burn the Fior mes Ivèrno settlement, and help destroy the Godless Ruins, they’ll be able to slay the god Sapadal, betray their companions, and formally join the Garrote.

While Fallout 4 did originally launch on the PS4, Bethesda did recently rerelease the game, complete with all DLCs, for all modern platforms, in the form of Fallout 4: Anniversary Edition.

Here, players embody a long-frozen survivor of both the Sino-American War and the Great War, who reawakens in the Commonwealth wasteland in search of their lost son who was kidnapped by a mysterious organization.

Throughout this journey, players can aid and join many factions such as the Minutemen and the Brotherhood of Steel, but easily the most villainous factions to align with in Fallout 4 are the Institute and the Nuka-World raiders. Both will continue to capture and experiment on humans and sentient synths alike.

FromSoftware’s Soulsborne titles are notoriously abstract with their storytelling, with even their endings often confusing players. There are still several ways to play more destructive, villainous roles in their games, leading to concrete chaotic endings, such as one seen in Elden Ring.

Similar to Dark Souls, Elden Ring has players embody an unnamed, reanimated being known as a Tarnished, as they set out to explore the Lands Between and strive to find a way to repair the titular Elden Ring, fighting multiple gigantic, monstrous bosses along the way.

While players can restore order to the Lands Between, they can also choose to destroy the world by defeating Mohg, the Omen and becoming imbued with the Flame of Frenzy by the Three Fingers, ultimately resulting in the Erdtree and the greater world’s destruction.

A list of ten soulslike games where the player turns out to be the villain by the end.

One of the best RPGs to debut in the ninth console generation was 2023’s record-breaking Game of the Year, the exploratory turn-based RPG Baldur's Gate 3.

Set roughly 100 years after the events of Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn, Baldur's Gate 3 stars a new player-character attempting to stop mind flayers, cure themselves of parasitic tadpoles, and stop the Absolute, otherwise known as the Netherbrain, from restoring the Illithid Empire.

However, players can ultimately take the Netherbrain’s power for themselves in the end, resulting in the citizens of Baldur’s Gate becoming mind flayers, dutiful warriors, or mindless fighters, among other dark outcomes such as the player simply killing everyone.

When it comes to finding a series full of brutal, often villainous protagonists, players would be hard pressed to find one darker than Warhammer 40,000. It’s filled with ruthless Space Marines that perceive any life that is not human as heretical and ripe for slaying.

While there are several great 40K games available on the PS5, there’s only one RPG from the series that debuted on the system, with that game being Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader. It stars the titular Rogue Trader, as they venture into the Koronus Expanse beyond the borders of the Imperium of Man.

Here, players can conquer alien worlds in the name of the God-Emperor or go rogue by aligning with the forces of Chaos, but no matter what path players go down, the people of the Koronus Expanse will surely suffer.

One of the most recent RPGs to allow players to dive headfirst into a truly despicable playthrough is Rebel Wolves’ debut title, The Blood of Dawnwalker.

Set in the fictional Eastern European kingdom of Vale Sangora after it was taken over by the Ancient Roman vampire Brencis, The Blood of Dawnwalker introduces the young half-human, half-vampire Coen of Laslea, as he sets out to save his family from the clutches of Brencis.

While Coen can be played as a heroic young warrior, players can instantly go about drinking the blood of everyone in the valley and even go so far as to make a deal with Brencis in the end. Even if Brencis is defeated, it might not have been a good choice in the long run, as the Black Death is said to return to the valley following Brencis’ death and the loss of his healing blood.

JRPGs sometimes put you on the other side of the good guy. Here are 8 PS2 JRPGs where you're actually the villain.

Without a doubt, the most villainous RPG PS5 owners can play as of the time of this article’s writing is Stunlock Studios’ V Rising.

Unlike the more altruistic half-vampire protagonist of Dawnwalker, V-Rising has people play as a monstrous, customizable, ancient vampire lord right from the get-go. They awaken from a 800-year-long slumber to reconquer the medieval steampunk land of Vardoran.

As a vampire lord, players can set out to say humans and monsters alike with a wide variety of weapons, spells, and vampiric abilities, but they can also build a living, six-story-tall castle that can be used to farm humans and animals alike for future thirst-quenching activities.

#4214. EU 'Digital Fairness Act' Could Have A Huge Impact On Loot Boxes And Virtual Currency

After being leaked earlier this week, the European Commission has today presented its proposal for the 'Digital Fairness Act' — a rule update that aims to offer "better protection for consumers and fairer competition for businesses" in the games industry.

To be clear, the proposal has not been adopted by the EU Commission just yet, but if it does go through, it could have a huge impact on several hot-topic game mechanics like loot boxes, virtual currencies, pay-to-win options and more. What's more, the act would apply to all EU member states without the need for individual approval.

So, what does the act set out to fix? The big notes that stand out to us appear in Article 15, which would require all companies offering "variable reward schemes" (or loot boxes, as you might know them) to be upfront about the items' contents and the probabilities of unlocking them. It calls for a requirement to toggle these options off in an "easily accessible manner," and no such items should appear in games designed for those under 18.

Likewise, Article 13 of the act prohibits personalised pricing based on user profiling — whether that profiling uncovers that the user is a minor, or if they are vulnerable to pricing practices in other ways due to their "age, credulity, disability, or any specific misfortune or circumstance of such gravity as to impair the consumer’s judgment".

Article 14 is all about virtual currencies, and it stipulates that companies must disclose "their estimated monetary value in the currency" to all customers. Any virtual-currency-related purchases must be turned off by default for minors, it continues, and can only be switched back on by a parent or guardian.

The Digital Fairness Act also proposes clampdowns on pay-to-win mechanics in games played by those under 18, and disabling toggles for any mechanics based on "[encouraging] compulsive or excessive use," like log-in bonuses and daily rewards.

Mechanics that fall under the umbrella of all the no-nos outlined above are subject to change, and the proposal states that the EU Commission will be able to add to the list at any time.

It's a rather dense read, and we struggle to see how many of the proposed changes would actually work in practice — how can you turn off pay-to-win strategies for under-18s and still keep things fair when playing against adults? — but it would certainly pose quite a change to the games industry as we know it.

With the soaring popularity of the likes of Fortnite and Roblox, it's only a matter of time before stronger unified regulations come into play. Whether those regulations end up looking like the Digital Fairness Act, and whether they actually protect customers, is another question entirely.

#4213. App Army Assemble: Momolitos - "Is this cutesy creature collector a worthy entry in the genre?"

Over the past few years, the main series Pokémon games have floundered somewhat, with Scarlet/Violet in particular being quite poor. As such, other developers have felt brave enough to put their own spin on the creature-collecting genre. Momolitos is the latest, and we handed it over to our App Army to get their thoughts.

Momolitos is a creature-collecting game with a wonderfully charming, cosy aesthetic. You'll spend time exploring different areas, gathering resources, and finding eggs and different types of food to feed, grow, and transform your Momolitos. Gathering and collecting come down to various minigames, which are all rather simple. The more you search, the more secrets you'll find, and Momolitos feels like it was all designed for you to discover at your own pace. Momolitos is the fresh take on creature-collecting I've been waiting for. A hidden gem in my 2026 playlist.

The game starts with no tutorial and no information on what to search for and collect. Once you enter the jungle, you understand. Collected multiple things in the jungle, but the player is stuck in the bottom right corner of the room. The game looks good, but you need tutorials and information. I would definitely try this game with a physical controller, but honestly not sure whether support is available or not.

Momolitos is a charming and simple creature collecting game. Gather wood, fish, vegetables and other resources while finding new creatures in order to feed and upgrade them and watch them evolve. It's got a nice art style and great gameplay. There's enough here to keep you busy and well worth its price.

This is a cute collect things and make creatures game. There’s a kind of fanciful land where you collect things, fish, and chop down trees. Most of that is pretty simple, but I failed at fishing. One fish appears, a brief flash of how to catch the fish, and I miss it. Walk around the lake for a while, miss another fish, and then I give up while waiting again. It’s a cute game that will, I’m sure, appeal to fans of the genre. But they lost me at the hard-to-get fish. Sorry.

Momolitos is a creature collector with simple animated cartoon graphics. You are situated in the MOMOlab, where you can teleport to an area to collect food and eggs. Back at the lab, you hatch the eggs and feed food to the creatures to make them evolve. The game opens up as you earn orbs.

As usual with a game available on other systems, the touch screen controls let the game down. Picking up food and eggs is very fiddly and frustrating. It’s a complex game with a lot to do, arguably too complex for a mobile game. I’d rather play this on my iPad and not on my phone. Not recommended for small screen devices. What is the App Army? The App Army is Pocket Gamer's lovely community of mobile game experts. As often as possible, we ask them for their thoughts on the latest games and share them with you.

To join, simply head over to either our Discord Channel or Facebook Group and request access by answering the three questions. We'll then get you in right away.

#4212. Award-Winning Composer And Musician Jon Batiste Talks Ocarina Of Time's Music And Why 'Guile's Theme' Goes With Everything

Jon Batiste has collaborated with the likes of Alicia Keys, Lenny Kravitz, Prince, Stevie Wonder, Willie Nelson, and many more. He performed the national anthem at Super Bowl LIX. He's headed up the musical efforts of The Late Show with Stephen Colbert. He's taken home more awards than we can realistically list in this article (including eight Grammys, as well as an Academy Award, a BAFTA Award, and a Golden Globe). But as I sit down with Batiste for a brief conversation about video game music, his energy transcends the Zoom call.

Before I can even ask a question, Batiste begins singing to greet me, then nerds out about my NBA Jam and Street Fighter II cabinets. He begins humming the menu music from NBA Jam and reminiscing about all the quarters he pumped into his local Street Fighter cabinet. The Louisiana native and Juilliard School alum has been an ardent gaming enthusiast for nearly three decades, with compositions from games like Sonic the Hedgehog and Final Fantasy VII inspiring his earliest musical endeavors. Spend enough time watching video game music performances on social media, and you'll likely soon find videos of Batiste sitting with famed Final Fantasy composer Nobuo Uematsu, or of Batiste performing gaming music.

With The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time delivering some of the most iconic music of all time (and Batiste famously loving the music), it makes sense that Nintendo would bring him out to New York to serve as a special guest at the launch event for the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2. I sat down with Batiste for a few minutes to chat about his love of video game music, his history with Nintendo, and why "Guile's Theme" from Street Fighter II just goes so well with everything.

Ocarina of Time is easily one of the most important video games ever made, and one of the things that makes it so special is the music. What about Ocarina of Time sticks out to you sonically?First off, if you want to get super inside baseball, technical music nerdery, which I love to do, in the compositions, there's a way that major chords and minor chords in... no sevenths, just root, third, fifth. They alternate, and it creates this magic that is, like, it's wistful, and it's simple. It feels ancient, and it feels like it's the music that is going on in your mind as you're generating thoughts and your imagination is churning. And the major chords are happening just after the minors in this contrary motion that's happening, so it feels like the music is going like this: It's going up – major, minor – like [sings the main Legend of Zelda theme song].

So, it's expanding and contracting, which is a musical allegory for the expansion and the openness of the world that Link is in. It's like [Koji Kondo] figured out how to capture the essence of the gameplay, but also the essence of magic and simplicity, which I think is really what makes... that's the music's power! So, you could listen to the music in the game, and you could also listen to it apart from the game and experience that magic.

Are there any tracks in Ocarina of Time that stand out to you as the most musically sophisticated or compositionally impressive?Oh man. Well, I think of it as a suite, so that's what makes it actually... there's nothing that's more or less complex, but the thought to figure out how to make all of the themes be interrelated yet singular. "Song of Storms" is, like, for me, that's a personal favorite. That's why I like to play it. I like to play a lot of the themes. That's how I grew up! I would play the game, and then, I would go to an instrument. Once we played for hours on Nintendo, we'd go and play Nintendo on piano! It was like a trade-off there, you know? I've been doing this since I was about 11 years old.

Taking it back to that 11-year-old Jon, talk to me a little bit about your history in general.Okay, so my history with Nintendo goes back to the NES. Christmas morning. Duck Hunt. You remember that? Maybe the first game I ever played. No, the first game I ever played was Donkey Kong, and then Duck Hunt, and then Super Mario Bros. Staples! We're talking about the early '90s. We had a room where I would go – it was my domain – and we had this blue shag carpet, and I would sit back there, and I would basically disappear into the carpet playing Nintendo for hours and hours.

And my mind is kind of... my mind can become a spiral; it can become a tornado. And I realized even then that going into this world of the game, even if I didn't win – it's not about winning or losing – it helps to organize the spiral of my mind and give me ideas and inspiration. So then, I started to get into Street Fighter II when I started to play more communally with my sister and my cousins. Yoko Shimomura, who I also had the pleasure of meeting and collaborating with, she composed incredible themes for each character, and that's when I really started to get a true love for fighting games.

And then, we would play so many of the Street Fighter franchise. We would play a lot of Final Fight. There were so many things... there was Double Dragon, then we got Mega Man... all these different series. Mega Man X is [an] all-time favorite. And then, here comes The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and that sort of expands the canon while also blending all of the elements: score, combat, the sort of linear quality of, like, a Donkey Kong or Super Mario World, and expanding the world in that way, expanding the canon in that way. Mind-blowing! So,  that sort of solidified my palate in terms of my favorite type of game.

You mentioned Street Fighter II. There's a meme about "Guile's Theme" and how it goes with everything. What about that composition makes it so it has the ability to enhance whatever video you pair it with?Wow! So, it has momentum in a way that is extremely [sings the melody of "Guile's Theme"] ... It draws you in, which is what you want [with] anything that you're starting when you're commencing a journey or watching something. You want it to draw you in, and that kind of pulls you in as that call and response. But it's an immediate announcement with the brass, and then the bass call and response. So, it's automatically giving you this feeling that something's happening, and I've got to pay attention to it! So that's the first step right there. And the tempo is really... it's a great tempo! It almost has the feeling of the great themes from, like, an '80s protagonist that's in a fighting movie. I think that was kind of the archetype. Yoko was probably drawing from that archetype, right? The action-hero archetype.

#4211. You're not crazy, trying to heal in Nioh 3 sometimes doesn't work - and Team Ninja is fixing it

One of the more insidiously aggravating bugs in Nioh 3 makes it so the game ignores you when you try to use elixirs, but hopefully not for long.

Nioh 3 has received a hot new update that brings plenty of bug fixes to very specific issues, but it also implements fixes for a few of the most common - and incredibly annoying - bugs. Patch 1.03.01 arrived earlier on all platforms, and it comes with a chunky set of notes.

This latest update, predictably, doesn’t add any gameplay features, but some of the included fixes will absolutely delight - or vindicate - so many of the game’s millions of players.

There’s plenty to go through in the patch notes published today for update 1.03.01, but the most impactful is a fix for an issue that “sometimes made it impossible to use elixirs during battle.” This is only a partial fix, but if you ran into the problem of smashing that shortcut button and not seeing your character play the healing animation, you’ll be glad to see it.

This is a problem myself and others have faced, especially in boss fights. You can even see the shortcut register your button press and proceed to ignore you. Another partial fix has been made to an issue that caused the game to crash. Team Ninja didn’t share specifics on that, and though Nioh 3 has been fairly stable for me in 70+ hours, it has definitely crashed a few times.

If you’ve been playing since launch, you likely have - or know someone who has - run into issues with save file corruption and other weird bugs around certain trackable items within save files.

Team Ninja already rolled out a couple of fixes there, and this latest one specifically targets losing valuables during Myths. If your save file has been affected, the game will now check and recover what was lost. Even more interesting is that the game will now automatically create a backup copy of your save data any time you load a save.

If you’ve made it into the Eternal Rift, you’ll be happy to know that today’s update takes care of a few progression blockers, and fixes an issue that allowed some players to obtain certain items before they were supposed to, locking themselves out.

One of the more amusing fixes concerns Mujina, who had a tendency to respawn if you prayed at a Shrine after opening a chest it was hiding in, which made it appear far more often than a mimic should.

Finally, there’s a set of fixes that address bugs (and exploits) when using specific Martial Art with certain weapons. There are a few fixes to AI, Myths, and one problem with the Minamoto no Yoritomo boss fight that made it impossible to interrupt him, even after he runs out of Ki.

Hit the link at the top for the full change log, and check out our Nioh 3 gameplay tips if you haven’t already. You should also change these settings ASAP, as they’re going to make your life much easier and save you a lot of time.

#4210. GTA 6 Was Almost Banned in Korea Ahead of Launch

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

Video games have always had an awkward relationship with age ratings, with a whole lot of legislation and systems only put in place after a game pushes the boundaries. Nowadays, it's incredibly common to find wanton gore and foul language throughout AAA titles, but sex and genitals are still treated carefully, only explored by a select few mainstream titles.

Microsoft's ad-supported Xbox Cloud Gaming service offers just 30 minutes of gameplay in exchange for three minutes of non-skippable ads.

Grand Theft Auto has never shied away from the debauchery of its cityscapes, utilizing nudity and sex in both optional and main story content. With the monumental Grand Theft Auto 6 sure to include even more while focusing on its protagonists’ love life, South Korean rating boards are having a tough time rating the game, citing a record amount of “out-of-context genital nudity.”

It feels like any game that tries to take notes from the Grand Theft Auto formula is required to feature some form of wanton nudity both narratively and mechanically. Saint’s Row, Cyberpunk, and one of Grand Theft Auto 6’s leak sagas even opened with fully nude gameplay of both protagonists, it’s just a feature of the subgenre at this point.

Despite this, Grand Theft Auto 6 almost got refused a rating in South Korea twice, a status that would have left it rudderless in the region. The main argument seemed to be less centered on story moments of nudity, and more on the purely functional moments of nudity. We already know that strip clubs have gotten a major overhaul, but being able to freely streak as both Jason and Lucia was a sticking point.

Regulators who fought for the title to instead earn the Adults Only rating, the age rating it ended up with, argued that while the visual fidelity of the title was vastly improved, there was no shift between Grand Theft Auto 5 and 6 that justified banning 6 when they allowed 5 without issue. From one regulator: “If we respect the precedent set for its predecessor, nothing has significantly changed other than sensuality.”

Grand Theft Auto has never shied away from the debauchery of its cityscapes, utilizing nudity and sex in both optional and main story content.

The first postponement the game was handed got botched due to delayed delivery of the playable build, leaving the regulators with less playtime than they had hoped. While the initial vote tied and this one was postponed for less-than-desirable playtime, the third was a resounding 8-1 vote in favor of the game’s Adults Only rating.

The biggest shifts in opinion came from finding that no sexual interactions were possible while nude, leaving it more of an absurdist comedy beat than potential erotica. The regulators were worried the game shifted its focus fully towards nudity and sexuality, only after ample playtime finding it kept the series roots as an action-adventure crime thriller.

The games industry has had a desire to be taken seriously by the rest of entertainment for quite a while, leaning into all different kinds of AAA design culture that has shifted and waned. The grey and brown color palettes of the 2010s, the walk-and-talk segments, moving away from boss fights and closer to cutscenes, and all kinds of focus pivots can be explained by this desire to be seen as ‘cinematic’.

Where Rockstar manages to avoid the downsides of these industry shifts is by staying insular, focusing so hard on their craft and their own design philosophy that they shift the industry around them. When you ask most casual players to think of a cinematic video game, they probably think of a Rockstar title.

It’s Rockstar’s world, and we’re all just living in it, if the unprecedented hype surrounding GTA 6 wasn’t enough to clue you in on that fact already. Breaking boundaries and keeping the entire world at attention, Grand Theft Auto 6 is truly looking to be the game of the decade.

Asphalt Legends Unite has covered some of the most famous automobile brands of all time. But one of their most well-known partnerships has been with none other than Ferrari. Now, the iconic Italian manufacturer is receiving its own dedicated season in Asphalt Legends!

Ferrari Season, which runs until December 9th, introduces three new iconic cars to the track in Asphalt Legends. Currently, the Ferrari F800 has the spotlight, while the Ferrari 849 Testarossa arrives until November 25th, and the Ferrari 296 GT3 Evo until December 2nd. All of these cars are faithfully recreated from their real-world counterparts down to the smallest detail.

The Testarossa, meanwhile, is a simple matter of completing increasingly challenging stages which themselves offer great rewards, with the end point being unlocking the car. Finally, the GT3 Evo has you competing against other players for the fastest time to, you guessed it, unlock this iconic supercar!

Ferrari may be out of reach for most of us, but we can all admire the craftsmanship and cutting-edge tech that goes into these cars. With these events ongoing until December, you'll have plenty of time to jump in and give them a go as well!

#4207. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – November 6, 2026

This week and weekend is all about the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, one of the few games I feel deserves the title of masterpiece. And the remake is really well done! I got every heart piece, every Gold Skulltala, the Goron Sword, and the biggest pouch for every one of my items over the course of the review... but I am contemplating jumping right back in for another go.

We also revealed our next cover and in case you missed the announcement it is... pause for effect... Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis! It's an awesome cover that celebrates the history of Lara Croft, and along with a cover story on the game, we also have a big retrospective on the series. I highly recommend subscribing to get your issue if you haven't already.

But it wasn't all just Zelda and Tomb Raider this week. Below you will find a list of weekend play recommendations, but before that... some of our biggest stories of the week.

We have been writing a lot about The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time remake this week because it is one of 2026's most exciting games, and it's real good. The remake is not particularly surprising. It mostly sticks to the trajectory of the original game, but there is a reason it is considered one of the best games of all time. It also looks and plays amazing.

You can read the full review here (or watch the video above), but we also have a big interview with the game's producers (one of whom worked on the original Ocarina of Time, and one who directed Breath of the Wild among many other Zelda games), some details about the Easter Eggs that did and did not make it into the remake, and a very handy tip for the game if you happen to be playing with a Switch 2 Pro controller.

World of Warcraft: Forever is out now and it’s a great time to jump into the revamped and expanded version of a project that changed online games forever back in 2004. A thousand new quests, multiple new zones, countless revamps, and an impressively stunning visual overhaul make it the perfect time to jump in for anyone who’s ever been curious to explore Azeroth.

2022's Escape Academy was a sneaky little puzzle game that surprised me and its sequel released this week. Taking place in a school obsessed with puzzles, you play as a student who must make their way through a series of escape rooms. The puzzles are clever, and the setting is charming, but the secret weapon is the local, split-screen co-op. Solving puzzles together is fun especially when one player needs to look at one section of a room to help dictate a solution on the other side of the room. My wife and I both love video games, but rarely play co-op games together just because of our disparate, individual tastes. But Escape Room is one we enjoyed together and we're so far enjoying the sequel. My only complaint so far is... I wish it ran a little better.

While we collectively use the term here for the sake of familiarity, I’m always a bit hesitant in my own mind to label a game under the wide banner of “Metroidvania.” In part, that’s because I think the two referenced games (Metroid and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night) are actually more different than they might appear at first glance. Gloomsoft’s recent release, Moadra, recognizes that distinction, crafting a game that draws heavy inspiration from the specific tradition of Super Metroid, even while presenting an intriguing and atmospheric fiction that is great fun to discover. In movement, actions, and exploration, Moadra feels remarkably similar to  the best of the 2D Metroid games. A scanning tool also leans into the Metroid inspirations, revealing details about the weird alien world you’re navigating. If you’ve been hungry for a game that scratches that particular itch of sci-fi gear/ability-gated exploration, I think you’ll find a lot to love in this game.

I get the Marvel fatigue we've all been experiencing. There are a lot of games and a lot of movies and a lot of TV shows and many are good, but lately most feel like homework. For those reasons, you'd be forgiven for dismissing the 2021 Guardians of the Galaxy game, but I promise you it is good. For one, it is standalone. It does not directly tie to any specific Marvel media. No homework necessary. And for two, it's just a really good game with an affecting story and a unique take on the characters that most of us met for the first time in the movies. And, for the BioWare fans out there mourning the loss of Mass Effect, this game has some Mass Effect energy. It's available on Switch 2 this week and I happily recommend it, especially if you missed it five years ago.

This exclusively two-player board game features a fun mix of activities. You act as both a dungeon architect, and an adventurer delving into said dungeons. Each player creates their own version of a challenging dungeon filled with traps, monsters, and treasures.

But you’re also forced to take on the dangers of your opponent’s crafted dungeon, to see who manages to come out on top. If you have fond memories of the hidden-info nature of old games like Battleship, but you want some greater strategic depth and fantasy flavor thrown in, this one is a great pick.

#4206. Genshin Impact Luna 5 takes the squad back to Mondstadt, finally makes Varka playable

Genshin Impact's next update will have you reminiscing about the good ol' days of... 2020.

The latest big content update has been revealed for HoYoverse's breakout game, Genshin Impact. Version Luna 5, which has the unusually long and needlessly layered title — Song of the Welkin Moon: Variation - Homeward, He Who Caught the Wind — is set to arrive February 25.

This one is a bit of a nostalgia play, taking everyone back to Mondstadt, the place where you may remember taking your first steps. And, as with any good return to the ol’ hunting grounds, come familiar characters, too.

The big new arrival is Varka, who joins as a playable character for the first time. Varka, Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius, is a character whose debut has been long-awaited. He is a 5-Star Anemo Claymore wielder with a dual-wield combat style, capable of dealing two different types of Elemental damage. His addition means that there's now finally a burly 5-Star male character of each elemental type... do with that information what you will.

Varka's dual-wielding combat style allows him to deal two different types of Elemental damage at the same time. The way it works is that his Elemental Skill boosts the damage of his regular attacks, but it also converts the damage type of his right-hand claymore to match his teammates’ elements (Pyro, Hydro, Electro, or Cryo). The left-hand claymore always deals Anemo damage.

The more normal attacks you use, the more frequently he can activate a special Elemental Skill, or trigger a Charged Attack that doesn’t consume stamina. He can also rely on the Hexerei effect to trigger more instances of Elemental Skill, as well as Charged Attacks, making him a monster damage-dealer.

Varka, of course, has been a staple member of the cast, featuring in both the original story in a small cameo, as well as taking a bigger role in the recent Nod-Krai chapters. With the return to Mondstadt, his playable debut makes sense. His Story Quest will shed light on his encounter with the Wild Hunt, and the Great Wolf King of the North

The reruns for this version are going to be Flins — who will be available in the first phase of Event Wishes — as well as Skirk and Escoffier in the second phase. You can also look forward to the return of the Chronicled Wish with Mondstadt characters.

Staying on the theme of reminiscence, the big event in Luna 5 is centered around revisiting memories from the beginning of your time with Genshin Impact, and reuniting with old friends. In Echoes of Memory, you’ll witness familiar scenes that have been changed slightly, and you’ll need to use the Spotter Kamera to detect and record those differences.

The Knights of Favonius are hosting several other activities for everyone to take part in, including an event that lets you catch up with old friends over drinks which you make for them.

Outside of events, there’s a new set of Gliding and Combat Challenges. And, of course, there are new minigames that you can relax with. The Kamera is being utilised yet again, and this time you can use to capture sights from your time in spots across Natlan, Fontaine, and Sumeru. There’s also… a horde mode of a sort, where you fend off waves of enemies.

#4204. Fredrik Wester Stepping Down as Paradox CEO in 2027

Lauren has experience in the gaming and esports space, writing news, guides, features, reviews, lists, conducting interviews, and more. Before joining the team at DualShockers, Lauren was a Features Writer at Adventure Gamers, a Guides Writer at Gameranx, as well as contributing as a News Writer at PCInvasion and Daily

Paradox Interactive, best known for being behind some of the biggest strategy games such as Age of Wonders, Stellaris, and Crusader Kings, has revealed that a change in leadership is on the horizon.

Fredrik Wester first served as the CEO of Paradox in 2009. He stepped down in 2018 to become Executive Chairman of the Board, but made his return as CEO in 2021, and will remain in position until the new CEO transitions in.

These strategy games don't bother making you feel like a hero.

The Board of Directors of Paradox Interactive announced on November 11 that Mattias Lilja, the current Deputy CEO of the company, will be the new CEO effective January 4, 2027. Wester, who informed the Board of his decision to step down, will become a member of the Board, focused on the future of the company.

The move has been called a “natural evolution of how the company is already led.” The statement continues, “Since 2021, Mattias Lilja has taken on increasing responsibility for operations and the execution of the company’s strategy, while Fredrik Wester has placed increasing focus on the company’s long-term development and goals. The company’s strategic direction remains firm, and Fredrik Wester remains the largest shareholder in Paradox.”

Wester says, “My plan was never to be CEO for life. The goal was to build the foundation before passing the baton on for the next chapter in the company’s journey.”

Lilja returned to Paradox when Wester took over as CEO in 2021, and in 2024, was appointed as Deputy CEO of the company. Wester believes Lilja “has had a central role in laying this foundation, and now is the right time to hand over. Given his experience and vision, he is exceptionally well-positioned to take the company to its next level.”

In relation to stepping into the role of CEO, Lilja explains that he intends to “approach this role with great humility. Paradox has a unique DNA that has made us one of the greats in deep and engaging strategy and management games."

As CEO, Lilja will be "stepping up the pace: we will make further investments in our core business, push the boundaries of our game design, work even more closely with our loyal players, develop more and better tools and services that benefit both modders and players, and continue to sharpen our ways of working and our organisation, with player value in focus.”

The Board of Directors of Paradox Interactive announced on November 11 that Mattias Lilja, the Deputy CEO of the company, will be the new CEO effective 4 January 2027.

Paradox has had a rocky ride with its new releases as of late. Europa Universalis 5 launched in November 2025 to mixed reviews, while the Across the Pillars DLC, which made its debut in October 2026, failed to impress fans. Paradox Tinto admitted that the team is “disappointed” with the release of the DLC, outlining: “we have put care, love, and a lot of effort into it, but it hasn’t turned out the way either you, the players, or us, the devs, would have liked it to be.”

As the publishers of Cities: Skylines II, this title also had a disappointing start when it launched in October 2023, but the developers have continuously worked on improving the game ever since through regular updates.

It will be interesting to see how future projects will fare under this new leadership. Paradox Interactive has a new strategy game in the works named Afterworld, for example, with a release date yet to be confirmed.

#4202. Nioh 3 is, unsurprisingly, the fastest-selling game in the series with over a million units sold

Nioh 3 has taken the Nioh franchise to new heights, delivering its biggest-ever launch.

Even before the game came out, it was pretty easy to guess that Nioh 3 would be a hit. From the word of mouth leading up to launch, to the well-received free demo, there was little chance the action RPG wasn’t going to be a major deal.

Today, publisher Koei Tecmo has announced that the game has officially passed over one million copies sold worldwide across PC, and PlayStation 5. This makes it the fastest in the Nioh franchise to reach this milestone.

As a result of this fantastic launch, Nioh 3 has now pushed overall Nioh franchise sales to be over 10 million, which includes the original Nioh as well as Nioh 2. Today’s news comes just two weeks after the game arrived on PC, and PS5.

On Steam, where it’s available on PC, it shot up the Steam charts, and immediately broke the series’ previous best peak concurrent player count record. From there, the numbers kept growing, leading up to a stellar weekend where it peaked at 88,045 concurrent players on Steam, double that of its launch day.

This now stands as the largest for any Nioh game on Steam, and though we don’t have insight into how well it’s doing on PS5 specifically, it still shows that the Nioh series continues to grow.

Nioh 3 builds on everything the two prior games established, and pushes the series into the semi-open-world realm, with several larger maps that each cover a period of time in Japan’s history. In our Nioh 3 review we called it “Team Ninja’s most accomplished action game, and the series’ most accessible.”

If you’re curious about the challenging and very rewarding action RPG, start with these gameplay tips, and don’t be shy to call upon a friend (or stranger) for help using our co-op guide.

#4201. Petit Planet Hands-On Preview – Creature Comforts

Petit Planet marks Hoyoverse’s maiden voyage into the life sim genre popularized by games like Animal Crossing, Stardew Valley, and, most recently, Pokémon Pokopia. The creators of Genshin Impact, Honkai: Star Rail, and Zenless Zone Zero have crafted well-received, lucrative free-to-play gacha games across several disparate genres; Petit Planet, fittingly, sees it try to attract yet another world of players. It’s been a year since I first played Petit Planet’s initial alpha test, and I spent a couple of more hours exploring its cozy cosmos at the Hoyoverse Media Tour in Seoul, South Korea. Although what I played has not dramatically changed my opinion of the game – it remains a delightful, if familiar, good time – speaking to its lead designer who goes by the single name Murphy and lead artist Yunli Huang helped shed light on how Petit Planet will differentiate itself from contemporaries and its approach to multiplayer, storytelling, and monetization.

The game’s premise centers on a customizable protagonist who sets out to populate their own personal planet (which is about the size of King Kai’s world from Dragon Ball Z). Although you are ostensibly human, everyone else is a talking animal. Your mentor of sorts is a chillax sheepdog named Mobai, who enjoys wearing straw hats and dropping his catchphrase/life mantra “Mo worries” and “Mo Rush.” The business-minded Glenn the Squirrel is a shopkeeper and seems like a cuter, less aggressive Tom Nook. Yunghou is a shy fox who enjoys farming and has the slightest hint of a southern accent. These critters and many more inhabit your planet, which you’ll grow from an empty (but vibrant) rock into a bustling village filled with homes, businesses, crops, decor, and, of course, neighbors.

Story is rarely a hook for a genre that largely promotes creating your own fun through the emergent moments with your neighbors and friends in multiplayer. Still, after Pokémon Pokopia presented an unexpectedly wild and fascinating tale, I ask if players should bother getting invested in a grander narrative à la Genshin Impact. The short answer seems to be “not so much.”

“Unlike other Hoyoverse games, there is no such main plot,” Murphy explains in my group interview. “There will be a main story at the beginning, but the main purpose is just to guide the players, get more familiar with the setting and the world. But the whole narrative of this game will be more fragmented. For example, if you look at those descriptions of those items, there will be a lot of content and narrative behind it. If you look at the description of creatures, many of them are real creatures in real world, and you get to learn more knowledge of this creature by reading those descriptions. And also, we've developed a very comprehensive narrative for each of our neighbors, so that is also part of our, called like, main plot, main narrative, because we want to make this world more like more lively and a more livable world. So that is how we treat narrative in this game."

While players who enjoy a substantial story to propel them through a game may be disappointed, those looking to unwind with a laid-back experience should be pleased. Hoyoverse is designing Petit Planet to be a no-pressure experience to enjoy at your leisure, hence why it emphasizes it as a life sim more than a management sim. There are no complicated stats to manage; simple inputs make it easy to pick up and play; imperfection is encouraged, with Hoyoverse comparing the experience to doodling as a child: your creation may not be perfect, but you had fun bringing your imagination to life.

I spent the first hour of my roughly two-and-a-half-hour session starting from scratch to see if any notable changes were made to this introductory portion in the last year. If there are any differences, they’re imperceptible because I wen went through the same onboarding of learning how to catch bugs and fish, building your first home, inviting your first neighbor, and farming crops, all while growing a magical sapling that, after performing enough tasks, blooms into a full tree that brings new life and mechanics to your world as it grows. Performing special tasks for residents, from completing requests to simply interacting with them, grows their bond, which, when high enough, will entice them to move in. For veteran genre fans, it’s a familiar song and dance. What I did notice this time around is how refreshingly quick the onboarding is. You have all of these foundational mechanics within the first 45 to 50 minutes, which is a nice pace. It was a good refresher for some foundational mechanics I’d forgotten since I last played, but it created an appetite to dive deeper.

Thankfully, Hoyoverse provided a second build set many hours into the game to give an idea of how planets can evolve. This build was set during winter, one of Petit Planet’s revolving seasons that alter the environment and introduce themed cosmetics and decor for players and residents. Sporting winter gear, I ran around the snow-covered planet, which was densely populated with shops, homes, and neighbors. I was initially greeted by unfamiliar faces named Trixie and Kookoo, who provided weather forecasts and news reports reminiscent of Isabelle from Animal Crossing and Callie and Marie from Splatoon. My sparse quest log was tricky to tackle since they revolved around mechanics I had no context for, such as setting up Vignettes. These are essentially templates for unique scenes filled out by dropping the correct furniture pieces in their layout; in this case, I had to set up an outdoor movie on the beach.

I only spent roughly an hour with this late build, and my biggest takeaway was simply how dense and lovely the village looked. A lot of work went into crafting this build, which boasted a farm filled with different crops (with unlockable recipes to create dishes from them), crafting tables to build furniture from collectible blueprints, and several shops, including Glenn’s to purchase a revolving selection of decor items. None of what I saw surprised me, however. Petit Planet so far checks many of the boxes you’d expect and want from a life sim. My cursory tour of a later-game planet did little to reveal any big new ideas, but what I did experience seemed perfectly cromulent.

My biggest question regards multiplayer. As much as I enjoy Animal Crossing: New Horizons and Pokémon Pokopia as solo experiences, playing with friends feels like a mean joke because of the tedious number of hoops to jump through just to invite other players into your world. And even once your buddy arrives, interactions are disappointingly limited. When I ask if Petit Planet offers a comparatively frictionless multiplayer experience, Murphy vaguely assures smoother sailing. “The multiplayer experience is a very important part of our game because, just as the interaction with NPCs, the interaction with other players is also a form of building up emotional connection to this game, and we want to provide that kind of experience to our players.” More specifically, Murphy cites features such as dynamic server load adjustments based on player counts and the option to allow or ban visiting players from taking resources from your planet to prevent griefing.

As a free-to-play Hoyoverse game, monetization is a major talking point. In Petit Planet’s case, the team agrees that rolling for neighbors gacha-style would be strange and defeats the spirit of the genre. Instead, all monetization will revolve around cosmetics; players can unlock new furniture and themed decor sets, outfits, and other cosmetic accessories for their character. Unlocking a full themed set of decor earns currency points, and there are myriad reward meters to fill for performing mundane tasks like greeting residents or catching bugs. It remains to be seen if and how Petit Planet’s progression begins nudging players into opening their wallets, but Hoyoverse promises it will be an experience that deemphasizes grinding.

I also briefly checked out the recently announced Switch 2 version of Petit Planet. My impressions after about 15 minutes of playtime: it’s fine. It sometimes ran noticeably hitchier than the PC version I spent most of my time with, but it seems perfectly adequate so far and, hopefully, will be a smooth experience when it launches sometime next year.

Since life sims require more than a couple of hours to fully reveal their quality, it was tough to get a read on Petit Planet even with this new showing. The game looks beautiful thanks to Hoyoverse’s signature sharp and colorful visual style. It has a relaxing vibe, and feels mechanically decent for the most part. In short, it seems broadly fine and like a respectable take on the genre. I suspect its biggest appeal will be that it will receive what Animal Crossing: New Horizons lacked: years of constant, substantial support.

Hoyoverse is very good about keeping fans of its games well fed with regular updates for years on end, and I don’t expect it to stop now. The idea of a seemingly well-made spin on Animal Crossing that’s free to download and, unless it completely bombs, will almost certainly receive years of new content is enticing on paper. I imagine this is the reason Petit Planet is coming to Switch 2 next year, where it can lure in Animal Crossing and Pokopia players before other consoles. PC and mobile players, meanwhile, must only wait until December 4 when Petit Planet fully launches to see if it has the chops to stand alongside the coziest giants of the genre.

#4200. Witcher 3's New Expansion Pairs Geralt's Polish Voice Actor With AI, But It's A "Special Case"

CDPR got the actor's blessing, after he suffered a stroke

The Witcher 3 is getting a brand new expansion next year titled 'Songs of the Past' and it's been revealed CD Projekt Red has used AI to help out with the voice work.

Before you get those pitchforks out, this is a "special case", according to the Polish developer. As highlighted by Game File reporter Stephen Totilo, CDPR called on the AI company 'Respeecher' to "record and tweak" the Polish voice of Geralt, Jacek Rozenek, after he suffered a stroke in 2019.

When the third expansion got underway, the team at CDPR wanted him involved but noticed his voice was "lower" and "gruffer", and feared it would be jarring for the player experience (swapping between the old and new dialogue). So with Rozenek's blessing, it got this AI company (which had previously worked on Cyberpunk 2077 after a VA's passing) to help make his performance sound more like it used to.

CD Projekt Red's head of localization Mikołaj Szwed shared the following comment with Game File about this decision:

"I do think this is one of those ways where you can use AI ethically, with consent and also do something good".

It's worth noting Doug Cockle will return as Geralt's English VA in the upcoming expansion, launching next year. This will follow the third game's remaster, which was released on the Switch 2 and other platforms in September.

#4199. The Sims 4 developer hasn't forgotten about its quality of life commitment, and is back with an update on what to expect in 2026

Maxis has offered some fresh details on its long-running mission to improve player quality of life in The Sims 4.

As the The Sims 4 continues into its second decade, the volume of new content, major expansions, and long-awaited features has grown in lockstep. Unfortunately, that has also meant that, given how old the game is, a few technical problems remain a nuisance.

The effort required to fix them is what led developer Maxis to make a commitment to improve the game’s technical state, and the developer has now returned to update the community on what to expect in 2026.

The quality of life pledge was made in September last year, through the introduction of a roadmap. Since then, the developer issued one update on its progress. Which brings us to this week’s new blog post, which further builds on everything that’s come before.

In the post, Maxis revealed a few key areas it’s going to be focusing on going forward. Though specific release dates for these changes were not shared, the list of issues should resonate with many players, as it covers many often-discussed topics.

The first stage of the new roadmap covers March through August. Over that period, you can expect Sims' autonomy to improve. This goes for things like how they choose locations for certain actions, they way they interact with certain objects, and even how often they interrupt conversations.

The infant and caregiver relationship is being updated, too, in order to improve autonomy and make sure your little Sims don’t miss out on milestones and interactions. That stage of the roadmap also includes fixes for black photo issues, and other crashes and freezing.

The next period takes place September through December, and it includes more interesting changes. One of the goals with this one is to improve Sims’ dining experience, which covers issues around eating and drinking.

Another important area of focus with this stage is family trees, and relationships between members of the same family. Maxis wants to improve the game’s genealogy systems to make relationship tracking across generations more robust so that your family history isn’t lost.

Depending on how the first stage goes, you might see more issues join the list of what the developer is looking at for the second stage of the roadmap.

The good news is that you won’t have to wait too long for the game’s next patch. Due out in March, this next update will feature around 55 fixes, including for some commonly reported issues.

Until then, you may want to check out The Sims 4’s Lost Legacies Event, which is available now until the middle of March. If you picked up the game’s latest expansion, check if you tried those Royalty & Legacy cheats.

#4198. Here Are Our Tips For Getting Starting In FM 27

Getting started in Football Manager can be tricky, especially with the wave of tutorials to navigate, so here are our tips to help you get started.

Getting into Football Manager 27 is a daunting task at the best of times. When starting a new game, you're met with a barrage of tutorials that are in place to teach you the basics of the game, but the reality is that you often have to figure things out as you go along. To help with this process, we've compiled a list of five beginner tips to get you started, make that overwhelming first hour of a save feel a

Before you even get into a Football Manager save, you're going to have to select the countries that you want to be part of in. This determines how many players are in the database at the start of the save and, more importantly, your PC's estimated performance in the game.

This will, of course, depend on the power of the PC or laptop you're playing on, but you rarely want to drop below "efficient" when it comes to game speed. This ensures that everything still runs relatively quickly, but there will be room for improvement. You can also add and remove leagues during a save, if you want to make an adjustment after starting a game.

It's been a long, hard road back to success for Sports Interactive, but FM 27 is the game I hoped it would be and so much more.

While your manager profile is somewhere you can be a little expressive, it also has an impact on your save. Whether you're playing it the realistic way, or want to enter the game as a managing prodigy, your decisions will have an impact on how your save will go.

For instance, selecting to start the game with no coaching badges will mean there are leagues in the world you simply aren't allowed to manage in until you earn them.

Elsewhere, your tactical focuses determine which attributes get a starting boost and what your board may expect of you early on. So, if you select that you're an expert in fast, attacking football, but then try to deploy slow, defensive tactics, you may find your team takes longer to adapt and grow into their roles.

It doesn't matter if you're brand new to the Football Manager franchise or a returning veteran; the introductions for each aspect of running a club are incredibly useful, and all of them are tailored to the club you currently manage. It's a great way to learn the ins and outs of tactical setups, team dynamics, training, scouting, set pieces, and more, while also understanding how each one applies to your specific club.

These rundowns give you an idea of your star players, those who may want to leave the club, the ongoing injury situation, your top transfer targets, and so much more. It's tempting to just blast through these introductions, feeling as though you can just learn as you go, but it will save you future frustrations if you pay attention to them at the very beginning of your save.

Identifying your best players should be a priority for every save. Yes, even before you decide on a tactic, because your best 11 (one per position) may create interesting dilemmas you can solve with tactical workarounds. If you try to stick to the same tactic for each save, you're fighting an uphill battle, especially if you have to try to sign players to fit the system every time.

By taking a close look at the club's best 11 players, you can figure out whether a one- or two-striker system is best; it will also tell you whether playing with wingers is possible and may reveal that playing five at the back is the way to go. Following the framework already in place when you join a club makes the first season much easier to approach, and you can gradually make changes over time, so you're more likely to see success.

FM 26 was a troubled game in many ways, but the move to Football Manager 27 won't force you to upgrade your gaming PC or laptop.

Your staff are the lifeblood of your club, but it's easy to overlook the staff situation when you start a new save; it should actually be a priority from the get-go. Checking your staff before you hit continue for the first time will help you identify any gaps you need to fill as soon as possible.

Thanks to the handy comparison tool, you can also see how your staffing totals compare with the rest of the league, so you know whether you're leading the way in quality or lagging behind. While replacing staff isn't cheap, it's a job well worth doing if you notice that your club requires big improvements to compete with the rest of the league.

You can then start scouting replacements via the recruitment screen, or, if you have a vacancy, post a job advert and see who applies for your open positions.

Now, this is going to look very different depending on which club you're taking over, but the first thing you should do on the financial front is adjust your budgets to suit your planned approach to transfers. If you're taking over a lower-league team that's tight on cash, you want to make sure you maximize your wage budget.

One thing that a lot of players don't realize, however, is that you can reduce your scouting budget directly into your transfer budget, and then you can make further adjustments if needed. This is especially useful for non-league teams in England, who may have up to £20,000 in scouting budget, but it's complete overkill, and you're better off feeding it into your transfer kitty to start making moves.

For richer clubs, you want to identify any major contract negotiations that will soon be required and, if so, make sure you have the wages available to action them.

The reason it's best to try to adjust your budgets ahead of time is that FM 27 can sometimes lock your budgets in place inexplicably during negotiations, which can cost you valuable transfers. So while you can't predict everything in advance, making rough estimates could save you headaches later.

At every opportunity, you should be talking to your players. This tip stretches beyond just the opening hour of the game, but it's something that not enough of us do, and it can be extremely helpful in the long run.

If players are performing poorly or well, be it in training or matches, speak to them about this performance and either praise or criticize it. This won't always be easy, as players with certain personality traits may surprise you with their response, but it will do more good than harm in most cases, and it can keep spirits up and your team motivated if you're constantly talking to them.

You should also be making the most of team meetings. Whether your recent form is poor or great, talk to the team and make sure you're checking in regularly. This is more important than ever with the introduction of Tactical Effectiveness, and your relationship with your players now plays a role in how well they pick up the tactics you implement. A stronger relationship can help them adjust to changes much faster and be more amenable to playing positions and roles they're not natural in.

The final tip is to scour your club for potential roadblocks or issues and deal with them as soon as possible. Unhappy players, financial issues, any agreed promises, fan distrust- whatever it may be- identify it and come up with a resolution as soon as possible.

The most likely problems you'll encounter relate to player happiness, and you can either force these players out of the club to prevent them from becoming toxic and impacting the rest of the squad, or reintegrate them to make them happy again.

This is going to be a more prevalent task if you're joining a club mid-way through a season, but some clubs have issues right from day one in FM 27, and it's your goal to make sure these problems don't get any worse.

#4197. GTA 6 Could Leave Millions of Desks Empty on Launch Day, Survey Suggests

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

If you were thinking about calling in sick on November 19 to spend the day exploring Vice City, don't worry: you're definitely not alone. In fact, a new gaming survey suggests that millions of Americans are planning to rearrange their work or school schedules for the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6.

And while some of us might have to get creative with our excuses, one company has decided to make things considerably easier for its employees.

According to a survey commissioned by PCMag and conducted by YouGov, approximately 12.5 million US gamers intend to take paid time off or adjust their schedules to play Rockstar's highly anticipated open-world adventure – that's around 8% of adult gamers in the country, which is quite a number for a game that hasn't even hit store shelves yet!

The survey questioned 2,024 American adults, including 1,154 people who identified as gamers, between October 23 and 27. Among those planning to make room for GTA 6, 3% intend to take at least two days off, another 3% are planning to take a full day, and 2% will either take a half-day or adjust their working hours.

As GTA 6's launch approaches, everyone wants part of the PR pie, including internet ISPs.

Interestingly, Gen Z appears to be the most committed group, with 13% of respondents in that generation planning to change their schedules. So, if your younger colleague suddenly disappears next Thursday, you might already know what's going on.

While most players will probably have to negotiate with their bosses to have some free time to play Rockstar’s title, Worldworthy has decided to take a different approach. The company, which publishes the Worldworthy 100 global rankings, actually announced that employees who want to play GTA 6 can take up to three paid days off starting November 19. No doctor's notes, questionable excuses, or suspiciously timed dentist appointments required!

Approximately 12.5 million US gamers intend to take paid time off or adjust their schedules to play Rockstar's highly anticipated open-world adventure.

"We decided not to fight it," founder and editor Ivgeni Zarubinski said in the press release sent to the media. "Everyone knows where a large part of the world will be next Thursday. Nobody on our team has to invent a dentist appointment."

Logitech wants employees to reap the personal and professional benefits of gaming.

The offer is optional, meaning employees who would rather keep working can do so, and the company's rankings desk will remain open throughout launch week. Still, it's a pretty generous way to acknowledge just how big this release is expected to be. Zarubinski even joked that after spending the year ranking the world's best airports, pizzerias, and cities, his team would get three days to "rank the streets of Vice City instead." To be honest with you, that's probably a much more entertaining assignment!

Of course, the survey also shows that the excitement isn't universal. Around 68% of US adults said they don't plan to play GTA 6 when it launches, while 14% intend to fit the game into their regular routines. Another 4% plan to clear their evenings and weekends rather than take time off.

Still, with GTA 6 arriving on November 19, it's clear that plenty of players are already making room for Rockstar's next adventure. The game follows the success of Grand Theft Auto 5, which has sold more than 200 million copies since its release in 2013. And if you're lucky enough to have a boss who understands the importance of visiting Vice City on launch day, maybe it's time to start planning that extended weekend!

A massive music festival will be held in Miami the weekend following the game's release, with numerous big-name performers to participate.

#4196. Genshin Impact fans on PS4 only have six weeks to find another platform as support winds down with one final update

Premium in-game purchases have now been disabled on PlayStation 4, as one of Genshin's four original launch platforms prepares to get dropped in early April.

Version Luna 5 of Genshin Impact is now live, but it's a bittersweet occasion for fans of HoYoverse's breakout gacha RPG – at the very least, those who are still playing the game on PlayStation 4, which is presumably true of somebody out there.

HoYoverse announced last year that they intended to wind down support for Genshin Impact on PS4, which – alongside PC, Android, and iOS – was one of the launch platforms for the game back in 2020. And with Version Luna 5, those end days are upon us.

The game has already been delisted on the platform since last September, meaning it was no longer available for download and could only be updated by players who already had it installed. But as of today, paid purchases from the in-game store have been disabled on PS4; and in six weeks' time, on approximately April 8, Version Luna 6 will discontinue access to the PS4 version altogether.

In many ways this is unsurprising – Genshin is already available on both PS5 and Xbox Series to sate fans eager to play on console, and the PS4's hardware is increasingly struggling to keep up with this massive open-world game after more than five years of regular updates have ballooned both its file size and technical requirements.

Aptly enough, Luna 5 takes the main story action back to the nation of Mondstadt, the location where the Traveler (and, by extension, the players) took their first steps into the world of Teyvat back in September 2020. It feels like a symbolic last hurrah for the original console home of the game, as does the inclusion of a Chronicled Wish banner focussing on some of Mondstadt's most iconic (read: too old to be meta by now) 5-Star characters – namely Eula, Mona, Albedo, Klee, Diluc, and Jean.

And as the icing on the Tea Break Pancake, this banner is running alongside the long-anticipated introduction of Varka – the Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius who has been a major character in the game's lore from the very beginning, but who only became playable with today's update.

Looking ahead to that post-Luna 6 future, Genshin Impact will still be available on PS5, as well as Xbox Series consoles, PC, and mobile devices – so hopefully anyone who is still playing primarily on PS4 will find another platform they can continue the adventure on by April.

#4195. The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin may be your next anime gacha obsession, with a hint of Ghibli, and this latest trailer may be what sells you on it

There's another free-to-play action RPG very much on the horizon. Will this be the one to win you over?

It seems like we’re getting one of these every few months, but the world of mobile action RPGs that look like the games that, just a few years back, were only possible on consoles is expanding with another new entry.

Netmarble, a studio and publisher known for its free-to-play games on mobile and PC, recently unveiled the launch date for The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin, its next major release that’s very much coming for the Genshin Impact crowd.

The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin is an open-world action RPG based on the world of The Seven Deadly Sins anime and manga. The game takes place in the world of Britannia, which looks similar to the way it does in the anime.

That said, the story of the game is not based on the anime or manga, Instead, it’s an original story set in the universe of the show. You play as Prince Tristan of the Kingdom of Liones who must find a way to bring order back to Britannia.

The gameplay should be familiar to anyone who played a free-to-play action RPG in the last decade. It features action combat, a roster of diverse heroes that you assemble to form teams, and a large pretty world to explore where you’ll also get to meet new characters.

Speaking of which, while Origin has its own original story, expect to be teaming up with characters from the series - some of whom wouldn't be able to meet naturally. You can thank the game's multiversal story for that.

Beyond all the serious business of saving the world and battling monsters, The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin also has a cozy, relaxing side. You’ll be able to fish, cook, forage and take on the beauty of the world with your pals.

The game has a bit of an unusual release schedule. It’s set to arrive on PC, PS5, iOS, and Android. PC (Steam), and PS5 players will be able to jump in starting March 16, whereas the global mobile launch is scheduled for one week later, on March 23.

You can pre-register right now on the official website if you’re interested in earning a few rewards when the game launches. You can, of course, always wishlist the game on Steam and the PlayStation Store, too.

#4194. Major World War 2 Flight Sim Goes Free for a Limited Time

News Editor at DualShockers, 10+ years writing experience, OpenCritic-listed reviewer, Master’s Degree in Developmental Psychology

The Il-2 Sturmovik name has become associated with excellence in flight sims since its initial release on November 18, 2001.

Although the team behind the first launch is no longer around, the torchbearers at For-Games are marking the occasion by letting new players try out the cornerstone game of the second generation of the Il-2 Sturmovik series.

Korea: Il-2 Series is a promising start for the next generation of flight simulators.

Starting today, Il-2 Sturmovik: Battle of Stalingrad will be free to play on Steam, as part of the 25th anniversary celebration of the franchise. The flight simulator is also offering an 85% discount until November 15.

Il-2 Sturmovik: Battle of Stalingrad centers on the battle of the same name that raged from July 1942 until February 1943. Although the Germans, led by the 6th Army, managed to enter the city, a massive Soviet counterattack led by Marshall Georgy Zhukov in November trapped Axis forces in.

Codenamed Operation Uranus, this move kicked off a brutal siege that would lead to the annihilation of the 6th Army and the capture of its commander, Field Marshal Fiedrich Paulus. The German defeat marked the end of its expansionism to the East, and is often cited as the turning point of the war in Soviet favor.

The fight on the ground has become the stuff of legends, but airpower played a major part in the battle of Stalingrad.

A massive German bombardment turned the city to rubble in August 1942, killing thousands of civilians and destroying almost all houses in the city. The German Luftflotte 4 averaged 1000 sorties per day between August 23 and November 22, 1942, putting immense pressure on the strained Soviet defenders.

When Zhukov's counterattack closed the door on the German troops in the city, the Luftwaffe pivoted from offensive missions to airlift, using transports and bombers to haul supplies and wounded. German fighters and attack aircraft managed to inflict heavy losses on Soviet units during this period, but were comprehensively beaten on a strategic level.

The fight on the ground has become the stuff of legends, but airpower played a major part in the battle of Stalingrad.

Soviet aviation in Stalingrad was outmatched in both quality and numbers when the Axis offensive hit in the summer of 1942. Reinforcements in August eventually helped tip the scale in the Red Army's favor, especially with the widespread deployment of La-5 fighters, plus Il-2 and Pe-2 attack aircraft.

The siege of Stalingrad allowed Soviet fighters to hunt down German transports trying to reinforce the 6th Army, in turn forcing German fighters to dedicate more and more time protecting these. Eventually, Soviet fighter activity pushed the Germans to primarily fly transports at night, which became increasingly prohibitive once the winter set in.

Meanwhile, Il-2 Sturmovik attack aircraft used the increasingly thin German fighter cover to pound enemy frontlines. Il-2 and Pe-2 units also took the fight to German airfields, hammering aircraft on the ground and helping seal the fate of the trapped garrison.

On its own merits, Il-2 Sturmovik: Battle of Stalingrad is one of the most realistic and advanced flight simulators in the market, and it remains the leading World War 2 game in its category.

Players are able to fly eight different aircraft in the standard edition.

On top of that, the Il-2 Sturmovik structure allows owners of any edition to play across maps in multiplayer servers, which means you’ll get to experience some of the newer maps if you choose to fly online.

Server owners like the Ad Astra group are setting up special events for free weekend players to help them get a feel for the game. This Saturday, Ad Astra is running a Siege of Odessa event set in August 6, 1941. Free weekend players will have access to the LaGG-3, Ju-87 and He-111. You can find more information on the by clicking here.

The Il-2 Sturmovik: Battle of Stalingrad free weekend event runs from 13:00 today until 13:00 on Monday, November 16, Eastern Time.

Il-2 Sturmovik: Battle of Stalingrad is part of the Great Battles series, first released in November 2013 and available exclusively on PC.
